lessonTitle: The Electrocardiogram: Waves, Rate and Rhythm

blocks.text: A 75-year-old woman tells her doctor her pulse feels 'all over the place', like a fish flapping in her chest. When the doctor takes her radial pulse it is fast and has no pattern at all: no regular beat, no regular pause. A 10-second ECG strip shows narrow QRS complexes bunched and spaced without rhythm and no P waves. The electrocardiogram turns the heart's electrical activity into a pattern we can read, and this one pattern has a name.

blocks.markdown: The electrocardiogram (ECG) records, from electrodes on the skin, the voltage changes produced by the summed electrical activity of the heart. Each wave marks a stage of the sequence of spread and recovery. The sinoatrial (SA) node depolarises first and spreads depolarisation through the atria. The impulse then reaches the atrioventricular (AV) node, where conduction is deliberately slowed, passes down the bundle of His and its branches to the Purkinje fibres, and depolarises the ventricles from the inside out. After contraction, the ventricles repolarise. The ECG is not a record of contraction: it records electrical depolarisation and repolarisation, and mechanical contraction follows.

blocks.title: ECG waves and intervals
blocks.text: The P wave is atrial depolarisation. The QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation (atrial repolarisation also occurs then but is hidden in the larger QRS). The T wave is ventricular repolarisation. The PR interval is measured from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS and reflects conduction from the atria through the AV node (the AV nodal delay). The QRS duration reflects speed of conduction through the His-Purkinje system and ventricular muscle. The QT interval spans ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation.

items: P wave: SA node fires and atria depolarise; the atria then contract.
PR segment and interval: the impulse is delayed in the AV node (typically about 120 to 200 ms for the PR interval; ranges vary by guideline).
QRS complex: rapid ventricular depolarisation through the His-Purkinje system; narrow (typically under about 120 ms) because conduction is fast and coordinated.
ST segment: all ventricular cells are depolarised (plateau of the action potential); normally level with the baseline.
T wave: ventricular repolarisation; it is upright in the same direction as the QRS in the leads where the QRS is mainly positive.

blocks.markdown: **Measuring on the paper.** ECG paper normally runs at 25 mm per second. One small square is 1 mm, equal to 0.04 s (40 ms). One large square contains 5 small squares and equals 5 mm, or 0.20 s (200 ms). Five large squares equal 1 second and 300 large squares equal 1 minute, which is the basis of the quick rate rules below. A standard ECG recording speed of 25 mm per second is assumed in all questions in this unit.

blocks.latex: \text{HR (regular rhythm)} = \frac{300}{\text{large squares between R waves}} = \frac{60}{\text{R-R interval (s)}}
blocks.caption: Heart rate in beats per minute from a regular rhythm at 25 mm per second. For small squares, use 1500 divided by the number of small squares.

blocks.title: Heart rate from a regular rhythm
blocks.prompt: On a regular rhythm strip at 25 mm per second, successive R waves are 5 large squares apart. What is the heart rate?

steps.text: Five large squares at 0.20 s each is an R-R interval of 5 x 0.20 = 1.0 s.
Heart rate = 60 / R-R interval = 60 / 1.0 = 60 beats per minute.
Check with the shortcut: 300 / 5 = 60 beats per minute, which agrees.

blocks.answer: Heart rate is 60 beats per minute.

blocks.title: Heart rate from an irregular rhythm
blocks.prompt: A rhythm strip covers 6 seconds (30 large squares) and contains 11 QRS complexes at irregular intervals. Estimate the rate.

steps.text: When intervals vary, a single R-R measurement is unreliable because the next interval would give a different rate. Count QRS complexes over a known time instead.
The strip covers 30 large squares x 0.20 s = 6 s.
Complexes per minute = 11 x (60 / 6) = 11 x 10 = 110 beats per minute.

blocks.answer: The average ventricular rate is about 110 beats per minute.

blocks.caption: Recognising common rhythms on the ECG.
rows: Regular, rate about 60 to 100 per minute
Every beat starts at the SA node
Chaotic atrial activity, variable AV conduction
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach)
Some P waves not followed by QRS
Progressively lengthens until a beat is dropped
Cycle repeats after the dropped beat
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
Some P waves not followed by QRS
Present at their own regular rate
P waves and QRS complexes independent (AV dissociation)

blocks.markdown: **Why these patterns arise.** In **sinus rhythm** the SA node paces the heart: a P wave precedes each QRS and the PR interval is constant. In **atrial fibrillation** the atria are driven by rapid, disorganised electrical activity, so there is no coordinated P wave; the AV node cannot pass every impulse, and it passes them at irregular intervals, so the ventricular rhythm is irregularly irregular. In **heart block** the fault lies in the AV node or His-Purkinje conduction. In first-degree block conduction is slowed but never fails. In second-degree block some impulses fail: in Mobitz type I each conduction takes longer until one fails, and in Mobitz type II there is no warning lengthening. In third-degree block no impulses pass, atria and ventricles beat independently, and the ventricles are driven by a slow escape pacemaker below the block.

blocks.title: Identifying a rhythm from features
blocks.prompt: A strip shows regular QRS complexes at 55 per minute and regular P waves at 90 per minute, with no fixed relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. Name the rhythm and explain.

steps.text: P waves are regular at 90 per minute, so the SA node and atria are working. QRS complexes are regular at 55 per minute.
P waves and QRS complexes occur at different rates with no fixed PR interval, so they are not related: impulses from the atria are not reaching the ventricles.
The ventricles are being driven by a slow escape pacemaker below the block, at 55 per minute.
This is third-degree (complete) AV block, with AV dissociation.

blocks.title: A systematic approach
blocks.text: Check rate, rhythm (regular or irregular), then look for a P wave before each QRS, the PR interval, QRS width and the relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. Sinus rhythm has a P before every QRS with a constant PR interval; atrial fibrillation has no P waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm; heart block shows a prolonged PR interval, dropped QRS complexes or complete dissociation.

blocks.title: The ECG is electrical, not mechanical
blocks.text: A normal-looking QRS does not prove the ventricle is contracting effectively. The ECG shows depolarisation and repolarisation. Do not confuse the P wave with atrial contraction or the T wave with ventricular relaxation: they precede and accompany the mechanical events respectively.

points: P wave is atrial depolarisation, QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation, T wave is ventricular repolarisation; the PR interval reflects AV nodal delay.

At 25 mm per second one large square is 0.2 s, so regular heart rate is 300 divided by the number of large squares between R waves; for an irregular rhythm count QRS complexes in 6 seconds and multiply by 10.
Sinus rhythm has a P wave before each QRS; atrial fibrillation has absent P waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm.
Heart block ranges from prolonged PR (first degree) through dropped beats (second degree) to complete dissociation of P waves and QRS complexes (third degree).

questions.stem: The PR interval on the ECG mainly reflects which process?

options.text: Conduction from the atria through the atrioventricular node
Spread of depolarisation through the ventricular walls

questions.correctOptionText: Conduction from the atria through the atrioventricular node

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the PR interval runs from the start of atrial depolarisation to the start of ventricular depolarisation and is dominated by the AV nodal delay.
distractorRationale.b: Ventricular repolarisation produces the T wave.
distractorRationale.c: The ECG shows electrical, not mechanical, events.
distractorRationale.d: Spread of depolarisation through the ventricles produces the QRS complex.

questions.explanation: The PR interval is measured from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex. It includes atrial depolarisation and the deliberate delay in conduction through the AV node, which allows the ventricles time to fill before they contract.

questions.stem: True or false: The T wave on the ECG represents atrial repolarisation.
questions.explanation: The T wave represents ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation occurs during ventricular depolarisation and is hidden within the larger QRS complex.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old reports palpitations. The pulse is irregularly irregular, and the ECG shows narrow QRS complexes at irregular intervals with no discernible P waves. What is the rhythm?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: absent P waves with an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm is the pattern of atrial fibrillation.
distractorRationale.b: Sinus rhythm has a P wave before every QRS and a regular rhythm.
distractorRationale.c: First-degree block has a P wave before each QRS with a long constant PR interval.
distractorRationale.d: Complete block shows P waves marching independently and a slow regular escape rhythm.

questions.explanation: In atrial fibrillation the atria are activated chaotically so no organised P wave appears. The AV node passes impulses unpredictably, giving an irregularly irregular ventricular response with narrow QRS complexes.

questions.stem: An ECG shows a P wave before every QRS complex, a regular rhythm and a constant PR interval of 0.24 s. What is the diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: every P wave conducts, but the PR interval is prolonged beyond about 0.20 s.
distractorRationale.b: In normal sinus rhythm the PR interval is within about 0.12 to 0.20 s.
distractorRationale.c: Mobitz type I has progressive PR lengthening and a dropped QRS, which is not described.
distractorRationale.d: Third-degree block has no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes.

questions.explanation: A constant PR interval above about 0.20 s (more than five small squares at 25 mm per second) with every P followed by a QRS is first-degree AV block. Conduction through the AV node is slowed but never fails.

questions.stem: A strip shows regular P waves at 90 per minute and regular QRS complexes at 40 per minute, with no fixed relationship between them. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Third-degree block: atria and ventricles are beating independently, the ventricles driven by a slow escape pacemaker
Sinus rhythm with a long PR interval
Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular rate
Mobitz type II block with a constant PR interval before each dropped beat

questions.correctOptionText: Third-degree block: atria and ventricles are beating independently, the ventricles driven by a slow escape pacemaker

distractorRationale.a: Correct: complete dissociation of P waves and QRS complexes defines third-degree block.
distractorRationale.b: A long PR interval would still have each P wave followed by a QRS at the same rate.
distractorRationale.c: Atrial fibrillation would show no P waves and an irregular rhythm.
distractorRationale.d: Mobitz II has a fixed relationship for conducted beats; here there is none.

questions.explanation: When P waves and QRS complexes occur at different regular rates with no fixed PR interval, no atrial impulses are reaching the ventricles. The ventricles are driven by a slow escape pacemaker below the block, which is third-degree (complete) block.

questions.stem: On a regular rhythm strip recorded at 25 mm per second, successive R waves are 3 large squares apart (each large square is 5 mm, or 0.2 s). Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
questions.explanation: Three large squares is an R-R interval of 3 x 0.2 = 0.6 s. Heart rate is 60 / 0.6 = 100 beats per minute, which agrees with the shortcut 300 / 3 = 100. This is at the upper limit of the usual resting range.

questions.stem: A 6-second rhythm strip (30 large squares at 25 mm per second) from a patient in atrial fibrillation contains 9 QRS complexes at irregular intervals. Estimate the average ventricular rate in beats per minute.
questions.explanation: The strip lasts 6 s, which is one tenth of a minute, so the rate is 9 x 10 = 90 beats per minute. In an irregular rhythm like atrial fibrillation a single R-R interval would be misleading, so counting QRS complexes over a known time gives a better average.

questions.stem: Relate the P wave, the QRS complex and the T wave to the electrical events of the cardiac cycle, and explain why the PR interval contains a delay and why atrial repolarisation is not seen as a separate wave.
markingGuide: P wave: depolarisation of the atria, spread from the SA node
QRS complex: depolarisation of the ventricles via the His-Purkinje system
T wave: repolarisation of the ventricles
PR interval includes AV nodal delay, allowing ventricular filling before ventricular contraction
Atrial repolarisation occurs at the same time as ventricular depolarisation and is hidden by the larger QRS complex
The ECG records electrical, not mechanical, activity
questions.explanation: The P wave is atrial depolarisation, the QRS is ventricular depolarisation and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. The AV node slows conduction so that ventricular filling occurs before contraction. Atrial repolarisation coincides with ventricular depolarisation, so it is hidden in the large QRS complex.

questions.stem: Describe the ECG features that distinguish sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation and complete (third-degree) heart block, and explain the physiological basis of each pattern.
markingGuide: Sinus rhythm: P wave before each QRS, constant normal PR interval, regular rhythm at about 60 to 100 per minute; SA node pacing
Atrial fibrillation: no P waves, irregularly irregular QRS; chaotic atrial activity with variable AV conduction
Complete heart block: P waves and QRS complexes independent (AV dissociation); slow regular ventricular escape rhythm; no atrial impulses conduct
May mention first-degree block as prolonged PR interval with every P conducting
May mention second-degree block as dropped beats, with or without progressive PR lengthening
questions.explanation: In sinus rhythm the SA node drives each beat, giving a P wave before each QRS with a constant PR interval. In atrial fibrillation there are no organised P waves and the AV node passes impulses irregularly, so the rhythm is irregularly irregular. In complete block no impulses pass the AV node, so atria and ventricles beat independently with a slow escape rhythm.

questions.stem: Explain how you would calculate heart rate from an ECG at 25 mm per second for (a) a regular rhythm and (b) an irregular rhythm. Calculate the rate for a regular rhythm with R waves 4 large squares apart, and for an irregular strip of 6 seconds containing 7 QRS complexes.
markingGuide: States one large square equals 0.2 s and one small square equals 0.04 s at 25 mm per second
Regular: rate = 300 / number of large squares between R waves, or 60 / R-R interval in seconds
Regular example: 4 large squares gives R-R of 0.8 s and rate 75 beats per minute
Irregular: count QRS complexes in a fixed time, such as a 6-second strip, and scale to one minute (multiply by 10 for 6 s)
Irregular example: 7 QRS complexes in 6 s gives 70 beats per minute
Explains why a single R-R interval is unreliable when the rhythm is irregular
questions.explanation: At 25 mm per second a large square is 0.2 s. A regular rhythm with 4 large squares between R waves has an R-R of 0.8 s, so the rate is 60 / 0.8 = 75 per minute. For an irregular rhythm the average is more reliable, so 7 complexes in 6 s scaled to a minute gives 70 beats per minute.
